vignette:
Marisol, a 50-year-old single jeweler in a small downtown storefront, was assaulted late one evening after closing, when she was locking the back door and a man she recognized from the neighborhood cut her off in the alley, grabbed her, and shoved her against the brick wall. What stayed with her most vividly was not the whole sequence but a few searing flashes: the cold slap of the wall, the sudden smell of his coat, the sound of her own breath turning ragged. Other parts of the event were strangely blank. She could not put the whole thing in order, and even now she would find herself pushing at the memory and then backing away before she could fully bring it into focus. At unpredictable moments, fragments would break through-a hand, the alley light, a sharp wave of nausea-and then vanish again. Those fragments were enough to make certain cues unbearable. If she caught sight of the offender across a street or in a store, her body reacted before she could think, and her awareness of danger narrowed immediately. Talk of people losing loved ones had taken on a similarly painful quality for her, because it pulled her mind toward the possibility that something precious could be taken without warning and left her feeling exposed and unsettled.

After the assault, Marisol began to judge herself harshly. She told herself that the way she reacted-jumping at ordinary footsteps, avoiding certain streets, freezing when she felt the slightest sick twist in her stomach-proved she was a lousy coper. She was ashamed that she felt contaminated by what had happened, as if the assault had left a stain on her that other people could somehow sense. That sense of being dirty and inadequate deepened her unease around other people. When someone she did not know approached her too quickly on the sidewalk, or when a man lingered near the jewelry cases in her shop, she became convinced that she was not safe. Her belief that she had handled the assault badly made her watchful for further danger; she read threat into ordinary encounters and felt most secure only in a very limited number of places, usually her own apartment or the back room of the shop with the door locked.

The memory and the fear kept feeding one another. Because she could not hold the whole event in mind without it breaking into fragments, she never felt it had been properly contained, and that unfinished quality made the triggers more powerful. Seeing the offender, hearing a discussion about bereavement, or suddenly feeling nauseous could bring one of those broken pieces back, and each piece reminded her that she had not really gotten away from the assault at all. When the memory surfaced, even briefly, she became more alert to danger in the present. She would scan exits as soon as she entered any room or building, choosing seats with her back to a wall and counting where she could move if someone came too close. In the shop, she positioned herself near the front so she could watch the doorway, but the vigilance was exhausting and made the day feel narrower. If a stranger paused too long near the display case or approached her with a question, she felt threatened at once, as though the alley were opening back up around her. That threat, in turn, made it harder to keep the fragments away; the more she felt on guard, the more the memory seemed to break through in flashes she did not invite.

Over months, Marisol's world contracted around these responses. She stopped lingering in crowded stores, changed the route she took home, and tried to avoid conversations that might bring up loss. At work, she had begun to rely on limiting her movements and keeping close to the safest corners of the store, which made her feel less present with customers and more detached from the craft she had once loved. She described herself as dead inside, not because she felt nothing all the time, but because the combination of numbness, shame, and constant alertness left little room for anything else. What finally brought her to seek help was an afternoon when a man she did not know entered the shop and stood too close while asking to see a necklace; she felt the sudden nausea rise, saw in an instant the alley wall and the offender's coat, and spent the rest of the day convinced he might come back. Marisol now says she wants to stop living as if every doorway hides another attack, but what frightens her most is that the fragments and the fear may never let her feel clean or safe again.
